items.summary: When a model achieves a new level on a leaderboard, what does that number actually mean? A benchmark auditor, a user researcher, and a SWE-bench co-author all read benchmark leaderboards, and none of them trusts the number at a glance. In this episode of Beyond the Leaderboard, host Janie Gu talks with three people close to AI benchmarks about what a score won't show you. Run the same tests on different infrastructure and the score changes because the benchmark measures the sandbox, not just the model. Frontier models can now recall entire repositories, which could lead to looking up answers instead of reasoning them. items.title: Companies Know What AI Costs But Not What It Buys
items.summary: In this episode, we’re joined by J.R. Storment, Executive Director of the Tokenomics Foundation and the FinOps Foundation at the Linux Foundation, to dig into the question every AI-heavy company is now facing: you know what you’re spending, but can you prove what you’re getting for it? J.R. explains what tokenomics really means (and why it has nothing to do with crypto). The real cost of AI goes well beyond API tokens. It includes harnesses, idle compute, storage, data, and the people who build and run it all. We look at how companies like Canva have had to rethink pricing as AI usage eats into cost of goods sold, flipping the old idea that more engagement is always good news. J.R. also shares findings from a survey of around 500 large enterprises. Most were confident they could see their spend, but 75% couldn’t show value their CFO would defend. Along the way, we cover engineers caught building their next startup on the company’s AI budget, why spend caps can actually push teams toward better decisions, the gap between activity metrics like merged PRs and real business value, why CFOs avoid the term ROI, and how model routing can backfire by breaking your cache. We also get into why not every problem needs an LLM, and how power shortages at data centers are quietly pushing up the cost of AI for everyone downstream. items.title: In an AI World, the Lab Matters More Than Ever
items.summary: "My style of physics has always been to go down to the basement and fool around with something and poke this and poke that and try stuff." Professor Peter Taborek is an experimental condensed matter physicist at the University of California, Irvine, and he mentions that he has followed his curiosity wherever it went. He was a student at Caltech, in the same class as Stephen Wolfram. He went on to Bell Labs, working under Nobel laureate Doug Osheroff in the days when a telephone company paid for fundamental research, and then to Texas Instruments, where he grew diamonds from a plasma at a time when many people doubted that was possible. At UC Irvine, he has studied quantum fluids and filmed cilia only a thousand angstroms wide beating around frog embryos. Along the way, Mathematica became one of his most important tools: he got one of the very first licenses on a NeXT computer, and computer algebra let him do calculations he could never have done by hand. Professor Taborek also cares a great deal about how science is taught. He found that the standard mathematical methods textbooks "basically ignored computers," so he wrote his own course, in which students work through problems in computational notebooks and learn to explain their results clearly, because in his view most of a scientist's career is communication. Now that AI "has read every book in the library and it's done every homework problem known to man," he thinks the human part of science is changing. He uses AI and is enthusiastic about it, but he doesn't think it replaces hands-on contact with the physical world, and he believes the lab "down in the basement" is where much of the action will be. His advice to young scientists who are anxious about the future is simple: "I think it's going to be okay."
